name: Sanchi
info: Sanchi is a hilltop Buddhist complex in Madhya Pradesh, India, whose Great Stupa was commissioned by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE and later enlarged and given four carved gateways.

facts.made: Commissioned by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka; enlarged under the Shungas; the carved gateways raised under the Satavahanas, with carving by ivory workers of Vidisha and donations from local people, monks and nuns
facts.form: A hemispherical dome, originally of brick and later covered with stone, on a high circular drum, with a railing, a crowning parasol and four carved gateways (toranas); the Great Stupa has about twice the diameter of the original
facts.where: On a hilltop at Sanchi Town, Raisen District, Madhya Pradesh, India, 46 kilometres northeast of Bhopal; some pieces are in the Sanchi Archaeological Museum, the Victoria and Albert Museum and the British Museum
facts.known: one of the oldest stone structures in India; four carved toranas; reliefs of the life of the Buddha and the Jatakas; the Buddha shown only by symbols; an Ashokan pillar with the Schism Edict; Brahmi donor inscriptions; UNESCO World Heritage listing

t: The Great Stupa began as a brick dome over relics of the Buddha under Ashoka, was enlarged to almost twice its size and cased in stone under the Shungas, and received its four gateways in the 1st century BCE and 1st century CE.

Its reliefs never show the Buddha as a human figure: he appears as a path, a footprint, an empty throne or a canopy under the bodhi tree, and local donors paid for the sculptures and had their names cut on them.

After Buddhism declined in India the monuments fell into disrepair; they were recorded by General Henry Taylor in 1818, ravaged by treasure hunters until 1881 and restored from 1912 to 1919 under Sir John Marshall.
dyk: Most of the Brahmi inscriptions at Sanchi are short records of gifts. In 1837 James Prinsep noticed that most of them ended with the same two characters, which he took as "danam" (donation), and this permitted the decipherment of the Brahmi script.
ev: Ashoka commissioned the Great Stupa, a brick hemisphere over relics of the Buddha
Under the Shungas the stupa was expanded with stone slabs to almost twice its size, with a railing around it
The first Buddhist reliefs were carved on Stupa No. 2, with mason marks in Kharoshthi
The decorated gateways began to be built under the Satavahanas, the earliest probably under Satakarni II
Chandragupta II's inscription was cut on the railing near the Eastern Gateway, and Temple 17 was built
General Henry Taylor recorded the site, overgrown but with several gateways still standing
Restoration under Sir John Marshall began and brought the structures to their present condition by 1919
The monuments at Sanchi were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

sections.origins:
Sanchi Stupa is a Buddhist complex on a hilltop at Sanchi Town in Raisen District, Madhya Pradesh, India, about 23 kilometres from Raisen town and 46 kilometres northeast of Bhopal. Its Great Stupa, also called Stupa No. 1, was originally commissioned by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. Its nucleus was a hemispherical brick structure built over relics of the Buddha, and the work was overseen by Ashoka, whose wife Devi was the daughter of a merchant of nearby Vidisha. Sanchi was also her birthplace and the venue of her wedding to Ashoka.

According to one version of the Mahavamsa, the Buddhist chronicle of Sri Lanka, Ashoka halted at Vidisha when he was heir-apparent and journeying as Viceroy to Ujjain, and there married the daughter of a local banker. She was called Devi and later gave Ashoka two sons, Ujjeniya and Mahendra, and a daughter, Sanghamitta. After Ashoka's accession Mahendra headed a Buddhist mission to Sri Lanka, probably sent under the Emperor's auspices, and before setting out he is said to have visited his mother at Chetiyagiri near Vidisa, thought to be Sanchi, where she is said to have had a sumptuous vihara built.
sections.content:
The Great Stupa, in its enlarged form, is a dome set on a high circular drum meant for circumambulation, reached by a double staircase. The dome was flattened near the top and crowned by three superimposed parasols within a square railing, a tiered form that was a symbol of the dharma, the Wheel of the Law. A second stone pathway at ground level is enclosed by a stone balustrade. Around the stupa stand four elabourately carved toranas, or ornamental gateways, which depict scenes from the life of the Buddha, events after his death, in particular the War of the Relics, and the efforts of Ashoka to spread the Buddhist faith.

The reliefs also illustrate Jatakas, the moral tales of the Buddha's former lives, among them the Syama, Vessantara and Mahakapi Jatakas, together with miracles and the temptation of the Buddha by Mara. In these scenes the Buddha is never represented as a human figure. His presence is shown by his path on the water, a chankrama or "promenade" slab hanging in the air, an empty throne, a footprint, a horse or a canopy under the bodhi tree. The complex also holds Stupa No. 2 and Stupa No. 3, a pillar of Ashoka with a Schism Edict, and temples from the Mauryan to the Gupta period.
sections.making:
The original stupa had about half the diameter of today's and was covered in brick. On the basis of the Ashokavadana it is presumed that the stupa may have been vandalised in the 2nd century BCE, an event some have related to the rise of the Shunga ruler Pushyamitra Shunga, and it has been suggested that Pushyamitra destroyed it and his son Agnimitra rebuilt it. During the Shunga period the stupa was covered with stone and the railings were added, dated to c. 150 BCE or 175–125 BCE. Some authors argue that the constructions of that period were not royal work: the dedications at Sanchi were private or collective.

The gateways were built from the 1st century BCE under the Satavahanas, who had taken eastern Malwa from the Shungas; the builder of the earliest is generally considered to be Satakarni II, who ruled in 50–25 BCE. Although made of stone, the toranas were carved and constructed in the manner of wood. An inscription on the Southern Gateway records that ivory workers from Vidisha did the carving. The reliefs at Stupa No. 2, dated to c. 115 BCE for the medallions, carry mason marks in Kharoshthi, which seems to imply workers from Gandhara in the north-west. The Ashokan pillar was carved from sandstone from the quarries of Chunar, several hundred miles away.
sections.reception:
The local population donated money for the embellishment of the stupa to gain spiritual merit, and there was no direct royal patronage at the gateways. Men and women who paid for a sculpture often chose their favourite scene from the life of the Buddha and had their names inscribed on it, which accounts for the repetition of particular episodes. Analysis of the donation records shows that many donors were local, while others came from Ujjain, Vidisha, Kurara, Nadinagar, Mahisati, Kurghara, Bhogavadhan and Kamdagigam.

Foreigners took part as well. Three inscriptions were made by self-declared Yavana donors, the clearest reading "Setapathiyasa Yonasa danam" ("Gift of the Yona of Setapatha"), and some friezes show devotees in Greek-style dress. The aniconism of the reliefs may conform to an ancient prohibition on showing the Buddha's body, known from the Sarvastivada vinaya. Sanchi art is considered the ancestor of the didactic forms of Buddhist art that followed, such as that of Gandhara, which added the Buddha as a man in Greek-style clothing. More precise details of exchanges or routes of transmission between Sanchi and Gandhara are elusive.
sections.survival:
Building continued until the 12th century CE, with Temple 45 the last Buddhist temple, built in the mid to late 9th century. With the decline of Buddhism in India the monuments went out of use and fell into disrepair. In 1818 General Henry Taylor recorded the site: the jungle had overgrown it, but the monuments were in relatively good condition and several gateways were still standing. Sanchi, on a hill, had escaped the Muslim conquerors who destroyed the nearby city of Vidisha. Sir Herbert Maddock clumsily breached the Great Stupa in 1822 without reaching its centre. Alexander Cunningham and Frederick Charles Maisey made the first formal survey and excavations in 1851.

Amateur archaeologists and treasure hunters ravaged the site until 1881, when proper restoration began. Major Cole reconstructed two gateways in 1882–83, and between 1912 and 1919 the structures were restored under Sir John Marshall. Nineteenth-century French and English interests wished to remove the Eastern Gateway; plaster-cast copies were made instead and the original stayed in the state of Bhopal, whose rulers Shahjehan Begum and Sultan Jehan Begum paid for preservation and a museum. A Gupta statue of Padmapani is in the Victoria and Albert Museum and one of the Yashinis in the British Museum.
sections.legacy:
Sanchi encompasses most of the evolutions of ancient Indian and Buddhist architecture, from the early stages of Buddhism and its first artistic expression to the decline of the religion in the subcontinent. The Great Stupa is one of the oldest stone structures in India, and about fifty monuments remain on the hill, including three main stupas and several temples. The reliefs, especially those depicting Indian cities, have been important in trying to imagine what ancient Indian cities looked like, and many modern simulations are based on them. The Sanchi pillar capital also belongs to a line of capitals running from the Pataliputra capital through the pillar capitals of Bharhut.

The relics found by Maisey and Cunningham were divided and taken to England, and Maisey's family sold the objects to the Victoria and Albert Museum. Buddhists in England, Sri Lanka and India, led by the Mahabodhi Society, demanded their return. Some relics of Sariputta and Moggallana were sent to Sri Lanka and shown in 1947, and the Chetiyagiri Vihara was built in 1952 to house them, an event that in a nationalistic sense marked the formal re-establishment of the Buddhist tradition in India. The monuments have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1989.

summary: Sanchi is a hilltop Buddhist complex in Madhya Pradesh whose Great Stupa, commissioned by Ashoka, was enlarged under the Shungas and given four carved gateways under the Satavahanas. It fell into disuse, was recorded in 1818 and restored in the early 20th century.
notes: start -250 with circa true: the article gives only 'the 3rd century BCE' for Ashoka's commission.
The lead says Devi was the daughter of a merchant of Vidisha; the Mahavamsa version says a local banker. Both are given, the second attributed to the Mahavamsa.
Stupa No. 2 and 3 order: the article says Stupa No. 3's gateway (c. 50 BCE per one passage, 1st century CE per another) differs; I left Stupa 3's gateway date out.
Pillar No. 26 (Lion pillar) is dated variously by the article (Ashokan in older sources, early Gupta, 600 CE per the museum); left out.
The Heliodorus pillar date varies (113 BCE, c. 115 BCE, c. 100 BCE); left out of the text.
The article's 'Satavahana inscription' identity of Satakarni is uncertain; I did not name the Southern Gateway architrave gift.
Left out: the Mahavamsa's Chetiyagiri identification beyond 'thought to be Sanchi'; the Reserve Bank 200 rupee note; Temple 40 and Temple 17 details.
Event 5th century: Chandragupta II's inscription is dated 412-423 CE and Temple 17 'probably first quarter of 5th century'.
